name: Fibermaxxing

card.summary: A social-media diet trend of pushing daily fibre intake to or beyond recommended levels with whole plant foods, followed for digestion, leaner body composition and the skin and energy that come with a well-fed gut.
card.note: Raising fibre too fast can cause bloating and gas; people with digestive conditions are advised to consult a clinician.

quick.overview:
Fibermaxxing means deliberately eating more fibre, aiming for or past the usual 25 to 38 grams a day, mainly from beans, seeds, oats, fruit, vegetables and whole grains. People follow it for a flatter-feeling stomach, steadier appetite and weight management, and for the skin and energy they associate with gut health.

The trend went viral on TikTok in 2025. Fibre's role in digestion, cholesterol and blood sugar is well described in nutrition research; the appearance claims are the community's own, and a Scientific American article raised the question of whether very high intakes suit everyone's gut.
quick.how: Followers add fibre-rich foods to meals rather than cutting foods out: chia or flax seeds, oats, chickpeas and other legumes, berries, avocado, and whole grains. Some set targets of 30 grams or more, and a few report aiming for 50 to 70 grams. Experts quoted in coverage advise increasing gradually and drinking enough water.
quick.risks: Increasing fibre quickly can cause bloating, gas, discomfort or constipation, and people with conditions such as IBS, Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis are advised by experts to check with a healthcare provider first. Purified fermentable fibres such as inulin can cause digestive distress at higher amounts.

lead: Fibermaxxing is a nutrition trend in which people try to maximise their daily intake of dietary fibre, usually by adding whole plant foods to meals rather than restricting anything. Followers tie it to digestion, fullness, steadier blood sugar and a healthier gut, and many hope for the leaner midsection, clearer skin and better energy that follow.[1]

The trend emerged in 2025, spreading on TikTok and X, where creators such as Pamela Corral posted fibre-rich meals like chia puddings; one of her posts was reported to pass 10 million views. It followed other 'maxxing' trends such as sleepmaxxing and smellmaxxing, and was covered by the New York Times by July 2025.[1]

Fibre's effects on cholesterol, blood sugar, regularity and satiety are documented in nutrition science, and typical American intake is well below guidelines.[1][2] A 2026 Scientific American article asked whether people with depleted gut microbiomes would benefit from very high intakes.[3]

chain: Eat more fibre from whole plant foods
Easier weight management and a leaner midsection
angle.text: People use fibermaxxing to feel full on fewer calories and keep digestion regular, which they link to a leaner, less bloated look. Some also expect the skin and energy benefits they attribute to a healthy gut; this is the community's claim.

infobox: Legumes, chia and flax, oats, berries, vegetables, whole grains

paras: Fibermaxxing promotes abundance rather than restriction. Popular foods include chia and flax seeds, oats, berries, avocado, legumes such as chickpeas, lentils and edamame, broccoli, sweet potatoes and whole grains such as quinoa and barley.[1]

US guidelines recommend 25 grams a day for women and 38 for men aged 19 to 50, and 21 and 30 for those over 50; the EU suggests 25 grams and the UK 30 grams for adults.[2] Adult Americans are described as averaging roughly 10 to 15 grams.[1]

The term's exact origin is unclear. It gained traction in mid-2025 through TikTok videos and the hashtag #fibermaxxing, and mainstream outlets covered it from July 2025.[1] Hacker News threads in 2026 show it continued to circulate, including coverage framing it as a trend nutritionists can accept.[4][5]

Soluble fibre such as oat beta-glucan and psyllium can lower LDL cholesterol; fibre also adds stool bulk, increases satiety and may help regulate blood sugar. High intake is associated with lower risk of colon and breast cancer and all-cause mortality, as associations rather than proven causes.[2]

Experts quoted in coverage generally say the benefits are well supported but that 'maxxing' can mislead, since rapid increases cause gas and bloating.[1] A Scientific American piece discusses whether depleted gut microbiomes may not benefit from superhigh levels.[3]

Fermentable fibres, especially isolated ones, can cause bloating, indigestion and flatulence, and inulin above about 15 grams a day causes distress in most people.[2] Experts advise gradual increases, hydration and clinician advice for people with digestive disorders.[1]
No studies found on fibermaxxing as a trend. Research on dietary fibre generally is extensive and covers cholesterol, blood sugar, bowel function and satiety.[2]

timeline.event: Fibermaxxing goes viral on TikTok and X.[1]
The New York Times covers the trend.[1]
Scientific American and other outlets examine very high fibre intakes.[3]

lore.intro: Fibermaxxing is discussed mostly on social media and in health press rather than appearance forums.[1]

claims.claim: More fibre improves gut health, fullness and weight control
claims.believers: Followers say adding fibre-rich foods keeps them full and regular.[1]
claims.experts: Nutrition references describe fibre as aiding satiety, bowel regularity, cholesterol and blood sugar.[2]

claims.claim: Going far past the guidelines brings extra benefit
claims.believers: Some users target 50 to 70 grams a day.[1]
claims.experts: A Scientific American article questions whether depleted microbiomes benefit from superhigh levels, and experts quoted in coverage urge meeting guidelines and ramping up gradually.[1][3]
